units.text: 16. Faith, meaning and alternatives to mechanism

When someone says the universe cannot be ‘just a machine’, they may express very different objections. They may demand an explanation for consciousness, defend freedom, assert a creator’s existence or reject the idea that a life’s value is exhausted by a physical description. We should not answer all of them with the same argument.

Theism can conceive order as dependent on a God who creates and sustains the world. Deism, schematically, emphasizes a creator and the autonomous operation of the created order. Other positions identify the divine with nature or attribute a more complex relationship to it. These orientations do not in themselves make the same prediction about experiments. A religious conception can be compatible with the same regularities accepted by a naturalist.

The differences may be metaphysical and existential without an immediate measurable consequence. But if a doctrine asserts that a particular physical event occurs under specified conditions, that component can be confronted with observation. Shielding an empirical claim with a general conception’s prestige is an error, whether that prestige is religious or scientific.

The problem of miracles shows the tension. If we define a miracle as violating a true and absolutely universal law, we have a contradiction by definition. If we define it as an unexpected event relative to known laws, it remains open whether we have an error, unknown mechanism or intervention. Hume analyzes justification for belief in miracles by weighing testimony against experience of regularities. Even those rejecting his conclusions can retain the methodological question: why should this account weigh more than alternative explanations? (Hume, 1748, sec. X.)

An advocate of a created world can legitimately ask why order exists. A naturalist may reply that introducing a creator moves the question: why does that creator exist and have those powers? Nor does ‘the laws simply exist’ eliminate explanation’s stopping point. The dispute also concerns what kind of endpoint is acceptable, not merely whether current knowledge has a gap.

Panpsychism, broadly, assigns fundamental status to experiential aspects or precursors of experience. It does not necessarily imply that stones think like humans or that our wishes alter instruments. It may try to answer a question about consciousness’s nature while remaining compatible with the same physical predictions. But that compatibility is not experimental confirmation of the thesis (Goff, Seager și Allen-Hermanson, 2022) .

Holism may demand that relationships and organization not be eliminated from explanation. This demand is sometimes indispensable. It becomes weak when it refuses to specify what difference the whole would make and how it could be investigated. ‘Everything is connected’ says too little: how, how strongly, at what scale and with what consequences?

Another alternative is process philosophy: what we call objects can be understood through the stability of processes rather than as substances wholly independent of change. We need not declare this orientation the final truth to use its question. A whirlpool persists through matter’s movement; an institution persists through activities and rules. When stability is produced, explaining it requires more than identifying a substrate (Seibt, 2022) .

In Beyond Good and Evil, §22, Nietzsche attacks how ‘nature’s lawfulness’ is presented as an uninterpreted text of the world. His challenge is that the concepts through which we read nature may carry preferences and values. We need not accept every consequence of his philosophy to hear the warning: even the ideal of a completely regular world may have a cultural history (Nietzsche, 1886) .

But this genealogy does not make every interpretation equal either. Two vocabularies may be culturally laden, yet one may enable far better predictions and interventions. Acknowledging interpretation does not mean abandoning reality’s resistance. The strongest critique preserves both levels.

Instead of automatic contempt or admiration, we ask what problem the alternative solves, what additional assumptions it makes and what would count against it. Some ideas will remain metaphysical; others will suggest experiments or disappear when precision is demanded.

Perhaps the world has a meaning physics does not formulate. Perhaps meaning is something beings construct in the world. Neither possibility entitles us to falsify an experimental result. Respect for great questions begins by not using answers too large for evidence too small.
